item.title: Tech Talks: Fact-Checking & Misinformation — Thu Nov 19, 3:30 PM — Montclair Main - Classroom
item.description:
Tech Talks is a free informational series where library staff introduce and explain the technology topics that matter most in today's digital world. Each session takes a closer look at a new or complex topic—whether it's a trending app, an emerging technology, or a platform you've been hearing about but aren't quite sure how to navigate. Through demonstrations and clear, jargon-free explanations, you'll come away with a better understanding of the tech landscape around you. There's no hands-on component, so no devices are needed—just come ready to learn and ask questions.
All are welcome regardless of experience level, and time is reserved at the end of each session for Q&A. Sessions are free and open to the public.
This week's topic is: Fact-Checking & Misinformation

item.title: Book Talk: Power Lines: Maps That Shaped the Way We See the World by Peter Keating — Thu Nov 19, 6:00 PM — Montclair Main - Conference Room
item.description: All maps show us where we are. Some maps also try to tell us what to think—and that’s where things get really interesting. In Power Lines: Maps That Shaped the Way We See the World (Black Dog & Leventhal, 2026), award-winning journalist Peter Keating presents a collection of maps that have defined borders, influenced social policy, and enacted political change. In Power Lines, Keating argues that the most dramatic and influential of all maps are political maps. Rather than reflecting geographical reality, political maps express man-made boundaries, territorial claims, and national identity. All the maps in Power Lines share two qualities: historical significance and persuasive power. Travel to ancient Greece to define existence; to the age of Exploration to express borders, identities, and ambitions; to antebellum America to track the ideas that paved the path to the Civil War; to the 1884 Berlin Conference to see Western leaders carve up Africa. item.title: Island Beach State Park — Sat Nov 21, 8:45 AM — NJ
item.description:
One of the gems of the state park system, Island Beach has miles of beach, tidal wetlands, maritime forest and thickets that can host a good diversity of birds, especially if the winds are right. November sees peak numbers of migratory waterfowl, loons, gannets, and other seabirds and is a good time of year for rarities. There is a $5 entry fee for NJ residents who do not have a state park pass or are 65 years of age or older. Be prepared for several hours of walking on flat terrain, sometimes sandy. Bring lunch. Led by Scott Barnes and Linda Mack. A NOTE ON MEETING LOCATION! We’ll meet just outside of the park entrance, in the median parking lot at the end of Rt. 35. PRE-REGISTRATION REQUIRED COST: $25 Members, $30 Non-members REGISTER HERE
Source: NJ Audubon

item.description:

We don’t allow formal instruction on our group-reserved courts, although giving some quick tips is OK so long as you’re not holding up others waiting to play.
⛑️ **Clinic Matches:** If we have to rotate people in then we may play some clinic-style matches where everyone rotates in evenly. There is no holding the court via wins so everyone has a chance to play regardless of skill level.
🕊️ **Early Bird Start:** If you want to meet earlier than 9 AM (like 8 or 8:30) then please let us know by the day before and we’ll see who can join you (usually I can do earlier).
**🎾 Equipment:** Please bring your own racquet and water, as we don’t provide those. I always have some balls for at least one court, but feel free to bring your own in case we need to branch out over more than one

item.description:
The Mindful Stream In these sessions, I will be doing guided meditations where we simply sit and notice what arises.
There is no agenda and no plan for how these sessions unfold. I might start off simply by asking us to notice what is already present. By becoming aware of what’s going on in our heads and in our body.
Then, the meditation may take on a life of its own.
Our job is to simply be present to what arises. We may notice the mind moving and chattering about. Or we may notice that it’s completely silent.
The goal here, if there is one, is to simply let ourselves be as we are.
